Act 1 · The seeing problem

What is computer vision?

Computer vision — teaching computers to extract meaning from images and video: what is there, where it is, and what is happening.
  • Image processing: image in → image out
  • Computer vision: image in → meaning out
  • Computer graphics: description in → image out
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The seeing problem · Day 1 · 12 / 128

1.12 · definition

The difference between the three is what goes in and what comes out. Vision is the hard direction.

Act 1 · The seeing problem

Computer vision is everywhere

01Phone face unlock
02Traffic enforcement cameras
03Pipeline corrosion inspection
04Crowd management at large events
05Medical scan screening
06Crop and palm-tree disease detection
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 1 · The seeing problem · Day 1 · 13 / 128

Act 1 · The seeing problem

The semantic gap

What you see

  • "A cat on a sofa"

What the computer sees

  • 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers between 0 and 255

The gap between these two is the whole field.

1.14 · compare

Write 150,528 on the board. Everything we do this week is about closing this gap.

Act 1 · The seeing problem

Why seeing is hard — 1

01Viewpointthe same car from the front and the side shares almost no pixels
02Lightingnoon and dusk change every number
03Scalenear and far objects differ in size by 10×

1.15 · cards

Why seeing is hard — 2

04Occlusionhalf the object is hidden

Images are just numbers

Before a machine can see, we need to know exactly what it receives

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 18 / 128

1.18 · section

This act is where most real-world bugs come from. Go slowly.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

The pixel

Pixel — the smallest unit of an image: one position holding one number (gray) or three numbers (color).
  • Zoom into any photo far enough and you reach a grid of squares.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 19 / 128

1.19 · definition

Show the zoom from a face to a grid of squares.

Worked example

Grayscale = a 2D grid

  1. A 5 × 5 grayscale image is a 5 × 5 table of numbers
  2. 0 = black
  3. 255 = white
  4. values in between = grays
  5. shape = (5, 5)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 20 / 128

1.20 · worked

Why 255? One byte holds 256 values, 0 to 255. That type is called uint8.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Color = three channels

  • Red channel
  • Green channel
  • Blue channel → stacked → one color image
  • shape = (H, W, 3)
  • Pure red = (255, 0, 0)
  • White = (255, 255, 255)
  • Black = (0, 0, 0)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 21 / 128

1.21 · diagram

A color image is three grayscale images stacked. Each channel is how much of that color is at each pixel.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Shape is the first thing you check

Grayscale photo(480, 640)
Color photo(480, 640, 3)
Color photo with transparency(480, 640, 4)
Batch of 32 color photos(32, 480, 640, 3)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 22 / 128

1.22 · table

Before you do anything with an image, print its shape. Half of all vision bugs are shape bugs.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Coordinates: the origin is top-left

  • (0, 0) top-left corner
  • x grows to the right
  • y grows downward
  • img[row, col] = img[y, x]
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 23 / 128

1.23 · diagram

This is the opposite of school graphs where y goes up. Slide 1.24 is the bug this causes.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Gotcha: x and y swapped

crop = img[50:150, 200:400]  # → rows 50–150 (y), columns 200–400 (x)

Writing img[x1:x2, y1:y2] crops the wrong region — and no error is raised.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 24 / 128

1.24 · code

No error, just a wrong crop. Silent bugs are the worst kind.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Data types: uint8 vs float

uint8

  • whole numbers 0–255
  • how images are stored on disk
  • small and fast

float32

  • decimals, usually scaled to 0–1
  • how neural networks want their input
  • precise
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 25 / 128

1.25 · compare

Models want floats around 0 to 1. Converting is called normalising.

Worked example

Gotcha: uint8 overflow

  1. Brighten a pixel: 200 + 100 = ?
  2. In uint8: 300 does not fit → wraps around → 44
  3. The bright pixel turns dark.
  4. Fix: convert to a larger type, add, then clip to 0–255.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 26 / 128

1.26 · worked

Ask the room to predict the answer before revealing 44. 300 minus 256 is 44.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Gotcha: BGR vs RGB

OpenCV loads images as B, G, R

Matplotlib, PIL, PyTorch expect R, G, B

Result: blue faces and orange skies · Fix: cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 27 / 128

1.27 · compare

This is the single most common bug in vision code. You will see it in Lab 1A on purpose.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Resolution and aspect ratio

01Resolutionhow many pixels (width × height)
02Aspect ratiowidth ÷ height (4:3, 16:9)
03Models usually need a fixed size, e.g. 224 × 224
04Squashing to a square distorts shapes; padding keeps them
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 28 / 128

1.28 · cards

When you resize a 16:9 photo to a square, a round wheel becomes an oval. Sometimes that matters.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Resizing needs interpolation

Nearest neighbour

  • copy the closest pixel
  • blocky, fast, keeps exact values (use for masks)

Bilinear

  • average the 4 nearest pixels
  • smooth, standard for photos
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 29 / 128

1.29 · compare

Use nearest for label masks so class numbers never get averaged into nonsense like class 2.5.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Other color spaces: HSV

RGB

  • how much red, green, blue

HSV

  • Hue (which color)

Saturation (how strong) · Value (how bright) · "Find the red object" = one range on Hue — even in shadow.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 30 / 128

1.30 · compare

In RGB, a red object in shadow has totally different numbers. In HSV the hue barely changes.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

Files vs arrays

JPEG

  • small, lossy, block artifacts, good for photos

PNG

  • larger, lossless, supports transparency, good for masks and diagrams

Once loaded, both are just arrays.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 31 / 128

1.31 · compare

Never save segmentation masks as JPEG; compression changes the class values at edges.

Act 2 · Images are just numbers

How models receive images

PyTorch

  • (N, C, H, W) — channels first

NumPy / OpenCV / TensorFlow

  • (N, H, W, C) — channels last
  • ToTensor() changes the order and divides by 255
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 2 · Images are just numbers · Day 1 · 32 / 128

1.32 · compare

N is the batch size, how many images go in together. Know which layout your library expects.

03

Writing the rules by hand

For decades, people designed every step of vision manually

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 34 / 128

1.34 · section

This act is history, but the core operation — convolution — is the heart of everything that follows.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Point operations

01Brightnessadd a constant to every pixel
02Contrastmultiply every pixel
03Inversion255 − pixel
04Each output pixel depends on one input pixel only
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 35 / 128

1.35 · cards

Point operations look at one pixel at a time and nothing else.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

The histogram

Histogram — a bar chart of how many pixels have each value (0–255).
  • Dark image → bars piled on the left
  • Washed-out image → bars squeezed in the middle
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 36 / 128

1.36 · definition

A histogram tells you about lighting without looking at the picture.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Histogram equalisation

Before

  • values squeezed into 40–120
  • details hidden

After

  • values stretched across 0–255
  • details visible

Used for X-rays, night footage, scanned documents

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 37 / 128

1.37 · compare

It spreads the values out so small differences become visible.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Thresholding

Thresholding — turning a grayscale image into black and white: every pixel above T becomes 255, every pixel below becomes 0.
  • Global — one T for the whole image
  • Adaptive — a different T for each neighbourhood
  • Otsu — picks T automatically from the histogram
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 38 / 128

1.38 · definition

Adaptive thresholding is how phone scanner apps handle a page with a shadow across it.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Neighbourhood operations

Point operations ignore neighbours. But meaning lives in neighbourhoods — an edge is a difference between a pixel and the pixel next to it.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 39 / 128

1.39 · rule

To see edges and textures, an output pixel must depend on a small patch of input pixels.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Convolution

Convolution — slide a small grid of weights (the kernel) over the image; at each position multiply the overlapping numbers and add them up. That sum is one output pixel.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 40 / 128

1.40 · definition

Multiply, add, slide. Say it three times. This one operation powers the rest of Day 1 and all of Day 2.

Worked example

Convolution by hand — the setup

  1. Image (5 × 5): every row is 0 0 0 9 9
  2. Kernel (3 × 3): every row is −1 0 1
  3. Output size with no padding: 3 × 3
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 41 / 128

1.41 · worked

The image has a vertical edge between the dark left and the bright right. Watch what the kernel does to it.

Worked example

Convolution by hand — the result

  1. Position 1 (columns 1–3): (0·−1 + 0·0 + 0·1) × 3 rows = 0
  2. Position 2 (columns 2–4): (0·−1 + 0·0 + 9·1) × 3 = 27
  3. Position 3 (columns 3–5): (0·−1 + 9·0 + 9·1) × 3 = 27
  4. Output row: 0 27 27 → the kernel lights up where the edge is
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 42 / 128

1.42 · worked

Flat regions give zero, edges give big numbers. The kernel is an edge detector.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · A kernel is a pattern detector

A kernel gives a large output where the image looks like the kernel, and near zero where it does not.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 43 / 128

1.43 · rule

This sentence explains CNNs. Keep it on the board.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

The kernel gallery

Box blurall 1/9averages neighbours
Gaussian blurcentre-heavy weightssmooth, natural blur
Sharpencentre 5, sides −1exaggerates differences
Sobel-x−1 0 1 / −2 0 2 / −1 0 1vertical edges
Sobel-ySobel-x rotatedhorizontal edges

Lab 1A runs every one of these on a real photo.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Edges

01Edge = where brightness changes sharply
02Gradient = how fast it changes (Sobel-x and Sobel-y)
03Edge strength = √(gx² + gy²)
04Canny: blur → gradient → thin the edges → keep strong ones and their connected weak ones
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 45 / 128

1.45 · cards

Canny is still used today in robotics and document processing because it is fast and needs no training.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Morphology — cleaning masks

01Erosionshrinks white regions, removes specks
02Dilationgrows white regions, fills small holes
03Opening = erosion then dilation
04Closing = dilation then erosion
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 46 / 128

1.46 · cards

(cut first) Useful for cleaning thresholded masks. One slide is enough.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Hand-crafted features

01Cornerspoints where edges meet — stable to track
02HOGa histogram of edge directions in each cell — the classic pedestrian detector
03SIFTdescribes a keypoint so it can be matched across photos despite scale and rotation
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 47 / 128

1.47 · cards

Engineers spent years designing these. They were the state of the art until 2012.

The classic pipeline

  • Humans design step 2
  • The machine only learns step 3
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 48 / 128

1.48 · diagram

The important part — what to look at — was decided by a human.

Act 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand

Where the hand-written rules break

01New lighting → thresholds fail

03New class → an expert must design new features
04Every task needs months of manual engineering
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 3 · Classical image processing — writing the rules by hand · Day 1 · 49 / 128

Supervised learning in one picture

That loop is all of training. Everything else is detail.

Train, validation, test

01Training setthe model learns from it
02Validation setyou tune choices with it
03Test setsealed until the end — the honest score
04Typical split: 70 / 15 / 15
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 56 / 128

If you peek at the test set while tuning, your final number is a lie. This rule is in your project rubric.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails

Loss

Loss — one number that says how wrong the model is on an example. Training means making this number small.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 57 / 128

1.57 · definition

High loss, bad model. The whole of training is pushing this number down.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails

Gradient descent

  • Picture the loss as a hilly landscape
  • The weights are your position
  • The gradient tells you which way is uphill
  • Take a small step downhill
  • Repeat
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 58 / 128

1.58 · diagram

You are blindfolded on a mountain; you feel the slope with your feet and step down.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails

The learning rate

Too small

  • tiny steps, training takes forever

Just right

  • steady progress to the bottom

Too big

  • overshoots, loss jumps around or explodes
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 59 / 128

1.59 · compare

The learning rate is the most important single setting in deep learning. Lab 1B has an extra task where you set it to 1.0 and watch it explode.

Worked example

From scores to probabilities: softmax

  1. Raw scores: cat 2.0 · dog 1.0
  2. car 0.1 → softmax → cat 0.66 · dog 0.24 · car 0.10
  3. Always positive, always sum to 1
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 60 / 128

1.60 · worked

Softmax turns any list of scores into probabilities.

Worked example

Cross-entropy loss

  1. True class: cat
  2. Model says cat 0.66 → loss = −log(0.66) ≈ 0.42
  3. Model says cat 0.05 → loss = −log(0.05) ≈ 3.0
  4. Confidently wrong is punished hardest
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 61 / 128

1.61 · worked

Cross-entropy looks only at the probability given to the correct class.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails

The obvious attempt: an MLP

  • Called a multilayer perceptron (MLP)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 62 / 128

1.62 · diagram

This is what anyone would try first. Let's see why it fails.

Worked example

Failure 1: parameter explosion

  1. Input 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers
  2. First layer of 1,000 neurons → 150,528 × 1,000 ≈ 150 million weights
  3. in the first layer alone
  4. More weights → more data needed → overfits easily
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 63 / 128

1.63 · worked

That is one layer. A real network needs many.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Failure 2: no sense of neighbourhood

Shuffle all the pixels of every image the same way — the MLP learns exactly as well. It never knew which pixels were neighbours.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 64 / 128

1.64 · rule

For an MLP, pixel 1 and pixel 2 are no more related than pixel 1 and pixel 50,000. But neighbours are where edges live.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails

Failure 3: move the cat, start again

Cat in the top-left

  • learned by weights connected to the top-left

Same cat in the bottom-right

  • completely different weights — must be learned again
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails · Day 1 · 65 / 128

1.65 · compare

An MLP must learn "cat" separately at every position. That is a huge waste.

Act 4 · Learning from data — and why the obvious network fails

What we actually need

01Locallook at small neighbourhoods
02Shareduse the same detector everywhere
03Hierarchicalcombine small patterns into big ones

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

A convolution layer

Convolution layer — a set of kernels whose numbers are learned during training. Each kernel produces one feature map showing where its pattern appears.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 68 / 128

1.68 · definition

Same multiply-add-slide as Act 3. The only difference is that training picks the numbers.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Local connectivity + weight sharing

MLP neuron

  • connected to all 150,528 inputs

Conv neuron

  • connected to a 3 × 3 patch
  • the same 9 weights reused at every position
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 69 / 128

1.69 · compare

These two ideas are why CNNs need far fewer weights and recognise an object anywhere in the image.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Convolution on a color image

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 70 / 128

1.70 · diagram

The kernel always spans all input channels. The number of kernels sets the number of output channels.

Worked example

Counting parameters

  1. Formula: (k × k × C_in + 1) × C_out
  2. Example: 3 × 3 kernels, 3 input channels, 64 kernels → (3·3·3 + 1) × 64 = 1,792
  3. The + 1 is the bias, one per kernel
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 71 / 128

1.71 · worked

Compare 1,792 with the 150 million from slide 1.63. Same input, a hundred thousand times fewer weights.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Padding

No padding ("valid")

  • output shrinks
  • 32 → 30 with a 3 × 3 kernel

Zero padding of 1 ("same")

  • add a border of zeros
  • 32 → 32
  • edges get processed properly
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 72 / 128

1.72 · compare

Without padding, every layer eats a border and edge pixels are barely seen.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Stride

Stride — how many pixels the kernel jumps each step. Stride 1 visits every position; stride 2 skips every other one and halves the output size.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 73 / 128

1.73 · definition

Stride 2 is a cheap way to shrink the image as we go deeper.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Dilation

Dilated convolution — spread the kernel's taps apart so a 3 × 3 kernel covers a 5 × 5 area with no extra weights.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 74 / 128

1.74 · definition

(cut first) Mainly used in segmentation for a wider view. One slide is enough.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network · The output size formula

Output = ⌊(W − K + 2P) / S⌋ + 1

W input size · K kernel size · P padding · S stride

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 75 / 128

1.75 · rule

This formula is in the exam and in Shape Race. Write it down.

Worked example

Output size — three worked cases

  1. W 32, K 3, P 1, S 1 → (32 − 3 + 2)/1 + 1 = 32
  2. W 32, K 3, P 0, S 1 → (32 − 3)/1 + 1 = 30
  3. W 32, K 3, P 1, S 2 → ⌊31 / 2⌋ + 1 = 16
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 76 / 128

1.76 · worked

Do the third one with them slowly. The floor is where people slip.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Pooling

Max pooling

  • keep the largest value in each 2 × 2 window
  • "was the pattern here at all?"

Average pooling

  • keep the mean
  • smoother

Both: 2 × 2 with stride 2 halves height and width, no weights to learn

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 77 / 128

1.77 · compare

Max pooling keeps the strongest response and throws away exactly where it was. That gives a little shift tolerance.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network · Why we need activations

Stacking linear layers gives… one linear layer. Without a non-linearity, a 50-layer network is no smarter than a 1-layer network.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 78 / 128

1.78 · rule

Two multiplications in a row are still just a multiplication. Non-linearity is what lets depth help.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

ReLU

ReLU(x) = max(0, x)
  • negatives become 0, positives pass through
  • simple, fast, and trains well in deep networks
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 79 / 128

1.79 · definition

ReLU is one of the reasons deep CNNs suddenly worked in 2012. Act 7 comes back to it.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

The classifier head

  • The conv layers find patterns; the head decides the class
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 80 / 128

1.80 · diagram

The body sees, the head decides. Transfer learning in Act 7 swaps only the head.

Input3 × 32 × 32
Conv 3→32, k3 p1 + ReLU32 × 32 × 32
MaxPool 232 × 16 × 16

This is the model in Lab 1B. Trace it with them line by line; the exam has a question exactly like this.

Worked example

Counting that network's parameters

  1. Conv1 (27 + 1) × 32 = 896
  2. Conv2 (288 + 1) × 64 = 18,496
  3. Conv3 (576 + 1) × 128 = 73,856
  4. FC1 2,048 × 256 + 256 = 524,544
  5. FC2 256 × 10 + 10 = 2,570
  6. Total ≈ 620 K
  7. An MLP on the same images (3,072 → 512 → 256 → 10) ≈ 1.7 M

What the layers learn

Nobody programmed this hierarchy. It emerges from training, and it looks like Act 3's hand-made kernels in the first layer.

Act 5 · The convolutional neural network

Receptive field

Receptive field — the region of the original image that one neuron can "see". It grows with every layer.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 5 · The convolutional neural network · Day 1 · 84 / 128

1.84 · definition

A neuron deep in the network sees a big area even though each kernel is only 3 by 3.

Worked example

Receptive field — worked

  1. One 3 × 3 conv · sees 3 × 3
  2. Two stacked 3 × 3 convs · sees 5 × 5
  3. Three stacked 3 × 3 convs · sees 7 × 7
  4. Pooling and stride make it grow much faster

Each extra 3 by 3 layer adds two pixels of view. This is why depth matters.

Batches, epochs, iterations

01Batcha group of images processed together (e.g. 64)
02Iterationone weight update, from one batch
03Epochone full pass through the training set
0450,000 images ÷ 64 per batch ≈ 782 iterations per epoch

CIFAR-10 has 50,000 training images, so that number is real for Lab 1B.

Act 6 · Training it properly

The DataLoader

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 89 / 128

1.89 · diagram

The DataLoader is a conveyor belt that hands the model one shuffled batch at a time.

Act 6 · Training it properly

The training loop, line by line

for images, labels in loader:
outputs = model(images)          # forward
loss = loss_fn(outputs, labels)  # how wrong
optimizer.zero_grad()            # clear old gradients
loss.backward()                  # compute gradients
optimizer.step()                 # update weights
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 90 / 128

1.90 · code

Five lines. Forgetting zero_grad makes gradients pile up across batches — a classic silent bug.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Reading learning curves

Underfitting

  • train and val loss both high
  • model too simple or not trained long enough

Good fit

  • both low and close together

Overfitting

  • train loss keeps falling, val loss starts rising
  • the model memorises
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 91 / 128

1.91 · compare

Always plot both curves. One curve tells you nothing.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Overfitting, explained

Overfitting — the model memorises the training examples, including their noise, instead of learning patterns that work on new images.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 92 / 128

1.92 · definition

Like a student who memorised last year's exam answers and fails when the questions change.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Fixes for overfitting

01More datathe best fix if you can get it
02Augmentationfake new data from old
03Dropoutrandomly switch off neurons in training
04Early stoppingstop when val loss stops improving
05Weight decaykeep weights small
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 93 / 128

1.93 · cards

Try more data and augmentation first. They usually help most.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Data augmentation

01Flip
02Random crop
03Rotation
04Color jitter
05Blur
06Each epoch the model sees a slightly different version of each image
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 94 / 128

1.94 · cards

Augmentation teaches invariance: a flipped cat is still a cat.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Gotcha: augmentation that lies

Safe

  • flipping cats, cars, X-ray texture

Wrong

  • flipping digits (6 ↔ 9), text, left/right road signs

Ask: does this change the true label?

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 95 / 128

1.95 · compare

Augmentation must never change the correct answer.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Dropout

Dropout — during training, randomly set a fraction of neurons (e.g. 50%) to zero each step. The network cannot rely on any single neuron.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 96 / 128

1.96 · definition

Like a team where any member might be absent, so everyone has to know the job.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Batch normalisation

BatchNorm — rescale each layer's outputs to a steady range (mean 0, spread 1) using the current batch, then let the network adjust with two learned numbers. Training becomes faster and more stable.
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 97 / 128

1.97 · definition

Keep it intuitive: it keeps the numbers flowing between layers in a healthy range.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Gotcha: train mode vs eval mode

model.train()

  • dropout on
  • BatchNorm uses batch statistics

model.eval()

  • dropout off

BatchNorm uses saved statistics · Forget model.eval() and predictions change randomly

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 98 / 128

1.98 · compare

Always call model.eval() and use torch.no_grad() before testing or predicting. This is in Spot the Bug.

Act 6 · Training it properly

Classification metrics

01Accuracycorrect ÷ total
02Precisionof everything I called "sick", how many were sick?
03Recallof all the sick, how many did I find?
04F1balance of precision and recall
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 99 / 128

1.99 · cards

Precision is about false alarms, recall is about misses.

Worked example

Why accuracy lies

  1. 100 X-rays · 95 healthy · 5 sick
  2. A model that always says "healthy" → accuracy 95%
  3. recall for "sick" = 0 of 5 = 0%
  4. Useless, with a great-looking number
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 100 / 128

1.100 · worked

On imbalanced data, always report precision and recall per class.

Act 6 · Training it properly

The confusion matrix

  • Rows = true class
  • columns = predicted class
  • diagonal = correct
  • off-diagonal = which classes get confused (e.g. cat ↔ dog, truck ↔ car)
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 101 / 128

1.101 · diagram

The confusion matrix tells you which mistakes the model makes, not only how many.

Reproducibility

01Set seeds for Python, NumPy and PyTorch
02GPUs can still give slightly different numbers run to run
03Record library versions
04A 1% "improvement" may just be seed noise
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 6 · Training it properly · Day 1 · 102 / 128

1.102 · cards

Before you celebrate a small gain, run it again with a different seed.

Change one thing at a time. Log every run: what you changed, the numbers, the curve. Save the best checkpoint.

01Data
02ImageNet
03Computetrained on GPUs
04ReLUtrains much faster than older activations

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 107 / 128

1.107 · cards

Three ingredients arrived at once. This is the moment deep learning took over vision.

Worked example

VGG (2014): just go deeper

  1. Idea
  2. use only 3 × 3 convs, stack many
  3. Two 3 × 3 layers see 5 × 5 (like one 5 × 5)
  4. weights: 2 × 9 = 18 per channel pair vs 25
  5. plus an extra ReLU
  6. Fewer weights, more non-linearity
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 108 / 128

1.108 · worked

Small kernels stacked beat big kernels. That idea is still used everywhere.

Act 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning

Inception (2014): many sizes at once

01Problemobjects appear at many sizes
02Fixrun 1 × 1, 3 × 3 and 5 × 5 convs in parallel and stack the results
031 × 1 convs shrink channels first to keep it cheap
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 109 / 128

1.109 · cards

(cut first) The 1 × 1 convolution trick returns in MobileNet.

Act 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · The degradation problem

Researchers made networks deeper — and training accuracy got worse. Not overfitting. The deeper network simply could not learn.

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 110 / 128

1.110 · rule

This surprised everyone. A deeper network could at least copy the shallow one and add layers that do nothing, yet training could not find that.

Act 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning

ResNet (2015): skip connections

  • Output = F(x) + x
  • The block only has to learn the change ("residual"), not the whole thing
  • If a layer is useless, it can learn F(x) = 0 and pass x straight through
  • Enabled 50, 101, 152 layers
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 111 / 128

1.111 · diagram

Learn the change, not the whole thing. ResNet is still the default backbone in many systems, including Day 2's detectors.

Act 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning

Why skip connections help training

01The signal has a shortcut forward
02The gradient has a shortcut backward
03Deep networks become as easy to train as shallow ones
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 112 / 128

1.112 · cards

The shortcut lets the learning signal reach the early layers without fading away.

ResNet-50 is too heavy for a phone or a camera chip. How do we keep accuracy and cut the computation?

Act 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning

Depthwise-separable convolution

Standard conv

  • each kernel mixes space and all channels at once

Depthwise-separable

  • Step 1 depthwise: one 3 × 3 filter per channel (space only)

Step 2 pointwise: 1 × 1 convs mix the channels

Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 114 / 128

1.114 · compare

Split one expensive job into two cheap jobs.

Worked example

The cost, worked

  1. Cost ratio ≈ 1/C_out + 1/K²
  2. K = 3, C_out = 256 → 1/256 + 1/9 ≈ 0.115
  3. About 8.7× fewer multiplications
  4. with a small accuracy drop
Computer Vision for Developers · Musa Ibn RashidAct 7 · Standing on giants: architectures and transfer learning · Day 1 · 115 / 128

1.115 · worked

This is a ceiling slide. The 1 over K squared term dominates, so 3 by 3 kernels give roughly 8 to 9 times savings.

01Deepermore layers
02Widermore channels

Transfer learning

Transfer learning — reuse a network trained on a huge dataset (like ImageNet) as a starting point for your own task, instead of starting from random weights.

Freeze or fine-tune?

Freeze the backbone

  • train only a new head
  • fast, works with little data

Fine-tune everything

  • small learning rate
  • best when you have more data or your images look different from ImageNet

Choosing a strategy

Little data, similar imagesfreeze, train the head
Little data, different images (X-ray, satellite)freeze most, fine-tune the last blocks
Lots of data, similarfine-tune all
Lots of data, differentfine-tune all, or train from scratch
